articles.headline: Microsoft Warnings Surface as Times Case Advances
articles.deck: Unsealed motion cites internal records on substitution, verbatim outputs and paywall workarounds.

pullquote.text: an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions

body: Unsealed filings in the case led by The New York Times describe internal Microsoft and OpenAI records on training artificial intelligence with news content. The motion for summary judgment quotes Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht warning that scraping was “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions” and perhaps the “largest theft of labor in human history”. News groups argue the documents show both firms understood the risk to publishers before releasing ChatGPT and Copilot.

ChatGPT head Nick Turley wrote that publishers faced an “existential threat” from products trained on news that substitute for providers. One Microsoft document described a “doom loop” “that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time.” Microsoft recorded 83 to 93 percent drops in click-through rates for some plaintiffs and 51 to 94 percent drops for others, alongside low click-through rates from ChatGPT search results.

Under oath Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said chatbots substitute for news by giving information on the platform instead of sending users to original sources. OpenAI engineer messages agreed users will not click even when links are shown. Internal messages also showed staffer Nick Ryder told President Greg Brockman a hack let crawlers get around the NYT paywall, and Brockman replied “Ah, nice.” News groups tested outputs by requesting summaries, bullet points and bias ratings and found extensive verbatim overlap.

A Microsoft spokesperson said the products are transformative fair use and do not substitute, calling Nadella observations on information habits and Hecht one employee perspective. Counsel Steven Lieberman, for the New York Daily News and seven sister papers, said the evidence shows the firms knew the conduct was wrong. Plaintiffs seek a ruling on articles with extensive verbatim overlap and argue substitutive copying weighs against fair use, with remaining claims reserved for trial.

art.caption: The exterior of the federal courthouse in Manhattan on a weekday morning. Cases over AI training on news content move through courts like this one.

articles.headline: Boston drops Flock cameras after nationwide data sharing
articles.deck: City officials cite a vendor error that exposed pilot data to outside agencies despite a contract limiting access to Boston police.
body: Boston abandoned its Flock Safety license plate reader pilot after data from department cameras became searchable nationwide. Mayor Michelle Wu confirmed the decision on GBH News. The city annual surveillance report for 2025 attributes the exposure to a vendor error. The contract required access limited to trained Boston Police Department personnel.

The department deployed about 45 Automated License Plate Reader cameras in a trial with Flock from April to September last year. Sharing was to be disabled under the pilot terms. Police confirmed with the company that settings were “off” for sharing. Within three days outside agencies could access plate and vehicle information through a nationwide lookup feature enabled in error.

The report states the program was designed to restrict access exclusively to trained department personnel. Upon learning of the error police had the function disabled. Further direct access required a written request to the department. No further direct access remained for the duration of the pilot. The report did not state how many outside agencies viewed the data.

The city did not end license plate reader testing. The police department started another trial with Motorola in February 2026. A third trial with Axon began in June 2026. City policy requires vendors to agree against sharing data. Recordings must be erased after 30 days unless police request retention for legal or investigative purposes.

Wu said continued use requires a publicly approved policy with privacy and civil liberties protections. “Yes, we need a publicly approved and authorized policy to guarantee all of those protections, privacy, civil liberties, and if that’s in place, then we should deploy technology to be able to keep people safe and solve crimes faster.” She said the department has tested versions to track vehicle movement. Officials seek clear limits on access, retention and storage time. She said the tool can aid safety when used responsibly.

An Electronic Frontier Foundation analysis of search logs described searches without legitimate justification. Flock said it added a dropdown list of crimes for searches in late 2025. The foundation said the change does not require proof of purpose. The company said new partnerships outpaced nonrenewals by approximately 10 to 1 so far in 2026. Other cities have dropped Flock. Wu said “When the toggles or the access controls either are not able to be restricted in the ways that conform with that policy, or are set but then can be unset or reset in ways that violate that policy, we would not use that platform.”

articles.headline: ChatGPT Lifts C Scores While Recall Slips
articles.deck: A controlled experiment with 55 students pairs higher coding scores with lower cued recall and reduced ownership.
body: Undergraduate programmers using ChatGPT-4.5 scored 89 percent on three introductory C tasks, compared with 69 percent for peers limited to conventional web search. The same assisted students recalled less of the material immediately and after 48 hours, and credited themselves with 45 percent of the submitted code against 81 percent in the comparison group.

The controlled between-subjects experiment retained 55 undergraduate computer science students for analysis from 59 participants. Each completed three tasks with ChatGPT-4.5 or web search without generative AI. Researchers measured task performance, self-reported mental effort and difficulty, pupillary responses, heart rate variability, and ownership, with cued recall tested immediately and 48 hours later.

Recall averaged 41 percent for ChatGPT users immediately after the tasks, compared with 53 percent for web search users. After 48 hours the figures were 39 percent and 52 percent. The loss of recall information over 48 hours did not differ significantly between groups. Self-reported mental effort increased less across tasks in the ChatGPT condition, with Holm-adjusted p equal to .047.

Confirmatory physiological tests did not detect significant differences in trajectories between conditions. The authors note substantial data loss limits interpretation of pupillary and heart rate variability results. Assisted performance therefore exceeded what students could reproduce from memory. The gap concerns task completion without retention or ownership. The study motivates assessment practices and AI learning tools that require students to explain, retrieve, and contribute to the work they submit as active participants in their education. High scores alone did not indicate learning in this setting. Code attribution and recall diverged from performance. Self-reported difficulty and ownership measures framed the difference as reduced cognitive investment rather than increased understanding. Performance was measured. Retention was tested. The distinction held. The machine completed the assignment. The student did not fully keep it.

articles.headline: Muse Tops ChatGPT Early Download Pace
articles.deck: Apptopia puts Muse at 1.8 million iOS installs in U.S. and Canada over first 12 days.
body: Estimates from Apptopia show Meta Muse outpaced ChatGPT during the first 12 days after launch on iOS in the United States and Canada. Muse recorded 1.8 million downloads in that subset, compared with 1.3 million for ChatGPT. The comparison aligns launch strategy differences, as ChatGPT launched globally on iOS only, while Muse launched in the United States and Canada on iOS and Android.

Apptopia also reports higher daily active use for Muse. In the United States, Muse reached 642,000 daily users across mobile, compared with 231,000 for ChatGPT at the same point. On iOS alone, Muse reached 359,000 daily active users, still above the ChatGPT figure. Overall, Muse saw 2.8 million total installs in its first 12 days. The app moved from No. 2 to No. 1 on the United States App Store, ahead of ChatGPT.

Apptopia provides third party estimates and does not have access to Meta internal figures. Meta has not shared public figures related to early adoption after a request for comment. The firm notes overlap with existing Meta services. Over 95 percent of Muse users are also Facebook users, and 63 percent are Instagram users. Muse connects with Instagram and Facebook and works inside WhatsApp. Meta used cross promotion and integrations for Threads, which now has more than 500 million users. Appfigures separately said Muse had crossed 1 million downloads. Business Insider reported the rise to the top store position on Friday.

articles.headline: Benchmark Tests 29 Models On Drone Decisions
articles.deck: PhysAI-Bench holds 10,178 UAV decisions with tool calls and 6G data, with top accuracy at 52.00 percent.
body: PhysAI-Bench evaluates foundation models on agentic decision making for autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles. The benchmark contains 10,178 standardized decision instances extracted from conversational traces of autonomous UAV missions. Each instance preserves mission context and sensor observations alongside Model Context Protocol tool calls and AI-native 6G network conditions. Twenty nine foundation models were tested. GPT-5.3 achieved the highest accuracy at 52.00 percent.

Each decision instance retains temporal dependencies and physical constraints. It includes Agent-to-Agent interactions and sensor observations. Network data cover latency, packet loss, throughput, edge load and network slicing. Only information preceding each decision is exposed. The design prevents future-event leakage and approximates online decision making.

The evaluation used a two-stage protocol with model-specific configurations. Twelve combinations of zero-, three-, and five-shot prompting and four temperatures were tested in three runs on a 35-instance, human-verified development set. Each selected configuration was then frozen and evaluated in three runs on a fixed, episode-disjoint set of 500 instances. Few-shot prompting generally improved performance. Temperature had limited influence.

Existing benchmarks assess physical perception, intuitive physics, embodied navigation and collaborative reasoning. They rarely evaluate the agentic decision making required for reliable autonomy. Autonomous UAV systems must perceive, reason, plan and act in dynamic environments. PhysAI-Bench targets that requirement with standardized instances and preserved context. GPT-5.2 scored 49.40 percent. Grok 4.5 scored 49.07 percent. The results demonstrate that reliable agentic decision making in Physical AI remains an open challenge. The dataset is available at the repository listed by the authors for further evaluation. Standardized extraction preserves mission context across episodes. Temporal dependencies link each decision to prior observations and tool calls. Episode-disjoint testing separates development material from final measurement. The protocol fixes each configuration before final runs to ensure direct comparison. Top accuracy doesn’t shift the final finding and the gap persists across all tested systems.

art.caption: A quadcopter flies above an open field at dusk. PhysAI-Bench evaluates such flights as sequences of mission decisions linked to sensors and network conditions.

articles.headline: Chatbot Defaults Keep Intimate Prompts for Training
articles.deck: WIRED finds enterprise deletion contracts offer the only strong shield, leaving most users with policy promises and proxy tools.

pullquote.text: You have this intelligent thing staring back at you, and you’re basically telling it, one question at a time, every possible thing there is to know about your life,

body: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini collect user prompts by default for storage, training and potential disclosure through legal process. WIRED reports that only paid enterprise and developer agreements provide deletion guarantees beyond policy promises. The report lists owners, partners, contractors, law enforcement and civil litigants as possible recipients of retained records with legal process for access.

Users treat the tools as therapists, sounding boards and virtual confession booths for health, finances, relationships and insecurities. That pattern creates detailed profiles built one question at a time from material once confined to private messages. WIRED notes that default policies place few restrictions on sharing, sale, further training or handover under court order or agency demand.

The strongest protection described is zero data retention, known as ZDR. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google offer ZDR in paid enterprise and developer accounts, with immediate deletion of interaction records after processing. WIRED states the option is unavailable to most individual users, who must rely on weaker policy promises not to log conversations.

Even ZDR includes exceptions for abuse monitoring. Anthropic withholds ZDR from Mythos-class models such as Fable 5.1, citing risks including scamming, hacking and autonomous misbehavior. OpenAI analyzes activity on customer systems before deletion under Private Safety Processing and can alert staff without revealing content. Google logs sanitized Gemini prompts without account identifiers, although identifying details in the prompt itself can still identify a person.

Consumer alternatives route or shield queries but depend on trust rather than technical guarantees. Proton offers Lumo for private conversation based on a no-log policy rather than end-to-end encryption. Venice.ai and Duck.ai similarly promise no logs while relaying requests to third party models, limiting direct collection by the underlying provider. Duck.ai allows selection of the model, while Venice.ai routes requests automatically without always disclosing the destination.

The exception built on cryptography is Confer, launched by Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to prevent server access to conversation content. The design uses technical controls to block surveillance and logging by the service itself, rather than relying on stated policy. WIRED positions the tool among a new group of privacy focused services offering anonymization, proxy routing or mathematical safeguards for users adopting chatbots for sensitive tasks. Stored records remain available to determined parties with legal authority unless deleted under contract. Disclosure includes training, sharing and sale without restriction. Control requires deliberate settings and selective disclosure. Default collection persists unless the user changes options or uses an enterprise agreement with deletion guarantees. Caution remains the most reliable control. The log remembers everything.

articles.headline: EU draft law phases social media access by age
articles.deck: Proposal ties safety-by-design defaults to EU age verification scheme.

pullquote.text: However they’re designed, age gates undermine civil liberties, reduce safety, and create barriers to internet entry, often at the expense of marginalized groups.

body: The European Commission draft Kids Act would phase social media access by age, require safety by design defaults, and expand age assurance across platforms and app stores. The Electronic Frontier Foundation says the plan puts services behind age gates and threatens privacy for all users. The proposal builds on the Digital Services Act and now faces scrutiny from lawmakers.

Platforms deemed risky would face a three tier system. Children under 13 would have no service accounts. Users from 13 to 15 would have restricted accounts under tight parental supervision. Users from 15 to 18 would have autonomous accounts in a safe by design environment. Risk status turns on personalized recommender systems or uninterrupted content consumption. Full online access is therefore reserved for adults.

Age delay depends on broad age verification. The system would rely on the EU age verification scheme. Parents would set up accounts for teenagers and prove parental status. Existing accounts would avoid repeat checks only if a provider can establish adult status with a high degree of confidence. Critics call that standard vague and intrusive. The Foundation warns companies will default to privacy unfriendly checks.

The second pillar applies beyond social media. It covers video sharing, online games, AI companions, chatbots and app stores. Providers must offer child safe design by default. Adult users could receive relaxed settings only after age assurance. Rules address infinite scrolling, account settings and recommender choice. AI services must limit emotional dependency and harmful interactions. Games must add contact protections. App stores would enforce age ratings.

Exemptions cover nonprofit encyclopedias, scientific repositories, educational services and open source software platforms. No clear exemption covers small and medium sized enterprises. Analysts say compliance costs will favor large technology firms. Decentralized networks such as the Fediverse face poor fit with centralized controls. Very large platforms must file compliance plans before launching new services. The Foundation says age thresholds remain a blunt proxy for maturity and reduce access to information and expression.

The draft avoids a blanket ban and distinguishes age groups and services. A French court recently rejected undifferentiated bans as unconstitutional. Supporters present the measure as hard law for nonbinding Digital Services Act guidelines on minors. The draft did not receive a full impact assessment with alternative options and stakeholder consultation. Lawmakers are urged to remove the most harmful provisions. The paperwork will be safe by design. Debate now turns to privacy, parental control and enforcement powers. Compliance costs will fall first on users and smaller providers.

articles.headline: Peer Support AI Improves Unevenly Across Communities
articles.deck: Training on the COPES dataset lifts strategy alignment by 50 percent, yet results differ across subreddits and coping strategies.
body: Post-training on the COmmunity-centered Peer Engaged Support dataset lifts strategy alignment by 50 percent for general-purpose models answering mental health queries on Reddit. The study evaluates zero-shot models against versions tuned with SFT and DPO using a three-axis framework centered on community perspectives. Gains in emotion and tone alignment accompany the strategy improvement. The improvement is uneven across subreddits and across requested coping strategies.

Researchers built COPES to measure lived-experience informed peer support rather than clinical benchmark performance. The framework assesses alignment with community perspectives on support seeking queries. It separates strategy alignment from emotion and tone and a third axis. Zero-shot baselines provide the comparison point for post-trained models.

The tuned models show stronger match to the coping strategies requested in posts. The average gain reaches the reported 50 percent for general-purpose systems. Emotion and tone move closer to community norms. The shift suggests training on community-driven replies teaches models what kind of help to offer and how to phrase it.

The gains are not uniform. Alignment improvement differs by subreddit and by requested coping strategy. Some communities see large increases. Others see small changes. Post-training also shifts the distribution of advice. Problem-focused recommendations increase. Emotion-focused strategies decrease.

Access to professional mental healthcare remains limited. Many individuals turn to Reddit for peer support situated within human lived experience. A significant portion of such queries go unanswered. The gap presents an opportunity for large language models to fill. Models have demonstrated strong performance on clinical benchmarks. Their ability to generate lived-experience informed and community-aligned peer support remains underexplored. COPES addresses that gap with community-driven data and evaluation tied to community perspectives.

Curating community-driven data improves alignment of responses. Performance remains disparate across distinct sub-communities and specific mental health needs. A model that matches one forum may miss norms in another. A model that handles requests for practical steps may weaken on requests for comfort. The bias toward problem-focused advice matters because peer support often involves acknowledgment and shared experience as well as suggestions. Suppressing emotion-focused strategies changes the texture of replies. It makes them more directive and less communal. The three-axis framework makes the tradeoff visible instead of collapsing quality into a single score. Developers seeking to deploy such systems will need to test by community and by strategy. Aggregate gains conceal local failures. The dataset points toward narrower tuning and closer attention to what each group asks for. The work records progress without claiming uniform coverage. Gaps still remain clear and measurable.

boxes.title: Performance Up, Retention Down
paras: ChatGPT-assisted students scored higher. The experiment enrolled 59 undergraduate computer science students. 55 were retained for analysis. Participants completed three introductory C programming tasks. One group used ChatGPT-4.5. The other used conventional web search without generative AI.

The team measured task performance and self-reported mental effort and difficulty. It recorded pupillary responses and heart rate variability. It tracked ownership. It assessed cued recall immediately and 48 hours later.

Generative AI can improve programming performance. Successful task completion may not reflect what students retain. The study examined performance, retention, cognitive load and ownership together. Higher performance did not guarantee retention. Ownership was reduced.

The design was between subjects. Measures included self-reports and physiology. Mental effort and difficulty were self-reported. Pupillary responses and heart rate variability were recorded. Cued recall was tested twice. The second test came 48 hours later.
The scope was three tasks. The sample was 59 students. The analysis was 55 students. The result is specific. Higher coding scores arrived with lower retention and reduced ownership.
Task performance was the first axis. Retention was the second. Cognitive load was the third. Ownership was the fourth. Each was measured separately. No single measure stood for learning.
The machine helped them finish. It did not help them remember.
